_provenance: Generated by eval/evidence_sufficiency/calibrate.py from real retrieve_and_rerank scores in scored_dataset.json (54 examples, grown from 40 in the prior session). Split seed: 42. Not hand-typed.

dataset.split_strategy: Stratified by coverage_type (FULL/PARTIAL/INSUFFICIENT), seeded shuffle (seed=42), approx. 46% calibration / 26% validation / 28% held-out test. AMBIGUOUS examples are excluded from all splits and reported separately. KNOWN LIMITATION: N=49 conclusive examples is still small - the held-out test split alone is too small to report a statistically robust accuracy on its own, which is why this script also checks the full-population confusion matrix as a sanity gate (see full_population_sanity_check below) rather than trusting the held-out split's number in isolation. No synthetic data was added merely to make the split look larger - every new example is grounded in real, previously-unused corpus text (see phase1_inspection.md's addendum).

candidate_approaches_tried: raw threshold (no adjustment, the ORIGINAL pre-Milestone-16 rule, kept for historical comparison only); CURRENT METHOD = logarithmic length penalty (score - alpha*log(length)), refit on the new split; CURRENT METHOD + SCORE GAP = the same plus beta*(top_score - second_score). Platt scaling / isotonic regression were NOT attempted - see why_not_platt_or_isotonic below.
why_not_platt_or_isotonic: Both need enough data to fit a probability curve reliably. With ~23 calibration examples (single-digit counts in some clause_type categories), a fitted sigmoid or isotonic curve would very likely overfit noise in this sample rather than capture a real relationship. A 1-2 parameter model is the most complex this sample size can support without the fit itself becoming a second source of fabrication - the same reasoning that ruled them out last session still applies at this only-modestly-larger sample size.
methodology_note_on_a_discarded_first_at: (From the prior session, preserved for context.) An earlier linear-penalty rule looked like a real improvement on a held-out test split alone but had an IDENTICAL confusion matrix to the baseline on the full pooled sample - it only relocated which examples were wrong. That is why THIS session's score-gap decision (see score_gap_experiment below) requires the gap variant to win on held-out test AND not be worse on the full-population check before it is adopted.

score_gap_experiment.hypothesis: A large gap between the top-ranked and second-ranked retrieved passage plausibly indicates a genuinely dominant, specific match, independent of clause length - this might catch cases the length penalty alone gets wrong (e.g. a long clause that is genuinely covered vs. one that only looks covered from length-inflated score noise).
score_gap_experiment.decision: ADOPTED - the score-gap variant beat the current method on the held-out test split and did not regress the full-population check.

full_population_sanity_check.note: NOT a held-out metric (the calibration/validation splits are part of this population) - a descriptive check that any adopted improvement is real across the whole sample, not an artifact of the small held-out split's composition.

Same legal content, extended with geographic scope and penalty language - still no corpus coverage regardless of length.

Adversarial case: heavy use of 'Kündigung'/'Vertrag' vocabulary that lexically overlaps with BGB Sec. 314 (termination), even though the actual legal question - post-contractual competition restriction - has no corpus coverage at all. Tests whether retrieval is fooled by lexical overlap into a false SUFFICIENT.
Same legal content, extended with usage-rights and pre-existing-IP carve-out language - still no corpus coverage.

The underlying confidentiality obligation itself has no corpus coverage, but the Vertragsstrafe (contractual penalty) mechanism for breaching it is specifically addressed by BGB Sec. 309 Nr. 6 - a real but narrow legal basis that covers the penalty clause, not the confidentiality duty it attaches to. A nuanced case showing topic-label coverage and mechanism coverage can diverge.

Same PARTIAL mechanism as penalty_for_confidentiality_breach (Sec. 309 Nr. 6 covers the penalty, not the underlying duty), extended to a MEDIUM length for the length-family pattern used elsewhere in this dataset.

An even longer variant of the existing confidentiality_* family (same genuinely-uncovered topic at every length) - added to stress-test whether the length penalty continues to behave correctly well beyond the lengths already in the dataset.

ambiguous_examples_not_scored_for_accura.coverage_note: Too generic to confidently map to Art. 28/32's specific processor obligations, but topically in the DSGVO domain the corpus does cover - a reasonable annotator could go either way.

Mixes a liability exclusion (clearly covered, Sec. 276/280/309 Nr.7) with a warranty-period shortening (also covered, Sec. 309 Nr.8b ff) in one paragraph - genuinely covered content, but classifying which single corpus passage 'is the' evidence is ambiguous, and the clause also touches on Vertragsstrafe fairness (Sec. 309 Nr.6), making this a defensible edge case rather than a clean FULL/PARTIAL call.

Extremely generic risk-allocation language - could be read as invoking Sec. 276's fault standard, or as too vague to map to any specific passage. A reasonable annotator could defensibly go either way.

A bare choice-of-law clause with no severability/incorporation content. Choice-of-law clauses in AGB can in principle be subject to Sec. 307 fairness control, but this single sentence has too little content to confidently say the corpus's AGB-control passages are 'the' relevant evidence versus irrelevant.

BGB Sec. 309 Nr.13 addresses form requirements for declarations TO the user (Verwender), not general contract-modification form clauses - close enough that a careless read might call it covered, but not actually the same rule. A genuinely close call.
